Claim: Czechoslovakia had a larger remaining Jewish population than most other Nazi-occupied countries during the Holocaust.

## Research findings

The claim that Czechoslovakia had a larger remaining Jewish population than most other Nazi-occupied countries is false and inverted. According to the US Holocaust Memorial Museum, Czechoslovakia's Jewish population was reduced from about 357,000 in 1933 to 17,000 in 1950 https://encyclopedia.ushmm.org/content/en/article/remaining-jewish-population-of-europe-in-1945 . The same source lists far larger remaining populations in other German-occupied/annexed countries: Poland reduced to about 45,000, Romania to ~280,000, with the Soviet Union retaining some two million Jews https://encyclopedia.ushmm.org/content/en/article/remaining-jewish-population-of-europe-in-1945 ; Hungary 445,000 in 1933 to 190,000 in 1950, Germany 525,000 to 37,000 https://encyclopedia.ushmm.org/content/en/article/remaining-jewish-population-of-europe-in-1945 ; France with 235,000 (250,000 in 1933), Italy 48,000 to 35,000, Greece 73,000 to 7,000, Yugoslavia 70,000 to 3,500 https://encyclopedia.ushmm.org/content/en/article/remaining-jewish-population-of-europe-in-1945 . Thus Czechoslovakia at 17,000 was smaller than Poland, Hungary, Romania, France, Germany, Italy, Austria (18,000) and others, not larger than most. About 80,000 Jews from Bohemia and Moravia alone were murdered https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Holocaust_in_Bohemia_and_Moravia (search snippet lines) , and >155,000 Jews passed through Theresienstadt with 35,440 perishing there and 88,000 deported to be murdered https://www.yadvashem.org/odot_pdf/Microsoft%20Word%20-%206359.pdf . The accompanying explanation that Nazis spared Jewish doctors is also contradicted by a 1946 Czechoslovak medical report quoted in Holocaust medical history stating 'all Jewish doctors were deported and most of them done away with' https://www.perlego.com/book/2095126/jewish-doctors-and-the-holocaust (search snippet) .

cascade.findings: The "It" is the Rose Garden Inn / Lighthaven Campus in Berkeley, bought by Lightcone Rose Garden LLC, which closed "on or about November 4, 2022" https://lawprofessors.typepad.com/files/ftx.pdf . FTX-group money did reach CFAR/Lightcone: FTX complaint lists $2,000,000 wired March 2-3, 2022 from FTX Trading Ltd to CFAR, plus "14 additional transfers to CFAR in the aggregate amount of $2,904,999.61" between March and Oct 2022, total "not less than $4,904,999.61" https://lawprofessors.typepad.com/files/ftx.pdf , also summarized as almost $5m transferred to CFAR from FTX Foundation https://hopzone.eu/forums/topic/47576-sam-bankman-fried-funded-a-group-with-racist-ties-ftx-wants-its-5m-back-silicon-valley/ . BUT: only part was for the purchase. Two $500,000 wires on July 13 and Aug 18, 2022 went not to CFAR but "from an account held by North Dimension to a title company as an initial deposit for Lightcone RG's acquisition" and were "intended as a loan to be re-paid once the financing...closed" https://lawprofessors.typepad.com/files/ftx.pdf . Oct 3, 2022 $1,500,000 grant (10 transfers) is only alleged "Upon information and belief, a material portion...was used...to fund Lightcone and the acquisition and renovation" https://lawprofessors.typepad.com/files/ftx.pdf . The bulk purchase funding was different: "$20 million loan" from Slimrock Investments Pte Ltd (Jaan Tallinn), including "$16.5m purchase price and $3.5m for renovations" https://hopzone.eu/forums/topic/47576-sam-bankman-fried-funded-a-group-with-racist-ties-ftx-wants-its-5m-back-silicon-valley/ , similarly described in complaint as deed of trust in favor of Slimrock which "provided Lightcone with a $20 million loan for the purchase and renovation" with total price $16.5MM https://lawprofessors.typepad.com/files/ftx.pdf . Timing "as it was collapsing" is also compressed: transfers span March-Oct, bankruptcy petitions were Nov 11 and Nov 14, 2022 https://lawprofessors.typepad.com/files/ftx.pdf , so March-July-Aug wires were months before public run/bankruptcy, only Oct 3 wires were ~5 weeks before filing. Claim implies sole funding by a last-minute wire to CFAR during collapse; record shows partial/contested funding over 8 months plus dominant Tallinn loan.

Why it is misleading:
- The deposits were made in July and August 2022 and the purchase closed in early November 2022. FTX collapsed in Nov 2022, so those deposits came months before the collapse and not 'as it was collapsing'. - The FTX funds are allegations in a complaint, and Lightcone disputes some of them. A Community Note on the article says Lightcone's CEO claims no FTX money came to Lightcone itself (https://commonnotes.net/).
- The money went to CFAR and to a title company, and the owner is the Lightcone Rose Garden LLC.

Claim: It was originally purchased with money wired to CFAR from Sam Bankman-Fried’s company, FTX, as it was collapsing.

## Research findings

The claim is partly supported but overstated and misleading. The article behind it is the Very Sane AI newsletter, and the property is the Rose Garden Inn, now Lighthaven, in Berkeley.

What the sources support:
- The FTX estate's complaint alleges that FTX Foundation wired $500k on July 13, 2022 and $500k on Aug 18, 2022 to a title company as a deposit on the Rose Garden Inn purchase. The purchase closed around Nov 4, 2022 (https://forum.effectivealtruism.org/posts/YSuqwrXFtuXuSzGDc/linkpost-sam-bankman-fried-funded-a-group-with-racist-ties). SFGate reports the same $1M allegation (https://www.sfgate.com/tech/article/sbf-berkeley-rose-garden-inn-19520351.php).
- The complaint says the transfers were meant as a loan that was never repaid. It also alleges that a material portion of other FTX grants to CFAR funded the acquisition and renovation (same EA Forum link).

Why it is misleading:
- The deposits were made in July and August 2022 and the purchase closed in early November 2022. FTX collapsed in Nov 2022, so those deposits came months before the collapse and not 'as it was collapsing'. Lightcone also says the purchase was made before FTX collapsed (https://www.greaterwrong.com/posts/9iDw6ugMPk7pmXuyW/lightcone-infrastructure-lesswrong-is-looking-for-funding/comment/vnYX8NPpHK4fRL5Gd).
- The bulk of the purchase was financed by a roughly $16.5–20M loan from Jaan Tallinn (https://forum.effectivealtruism.org/posts/rsnrpvKofps5Py7di/shutting-down-the-lightcone-offices). FTX money covered only a small part.
- The FTX funds are allegations in a complaint, and Lightcone disputes some of them. A Community Note on the article says Lightcone's CEO claims no FTX money came to Lightcone itself (https://commonnotes.net/).
- The money went to CFAR and to a title company, and the owner is the Lightcone Rose Garden LLC.
- 'Originally purchased with money wired…' implies FTX money was the main source, which is overstated.

samples.research:
The claim is probably about the Rose Garden Inn, now Lighthaven, in Berkeley. It is partly accurate but oversimplified. The FTX estate's complaint, as quoted on the EA Forum, says the FTX Foundation wired two $500,000 payments (July 13 and August 18, 2022) from North Dimension accounts to a title company as a deposit for Lightcone RG's purchase of the Rose Garden Inn (https://forum.effectivealtruism.org/posts/YSuqwrXFtuXuSzGDc/linkpost-sam-bankman-fried-funded-a-group-with-racist-ties). The same complaint says the sale closed around Nov 4, 2022, and that a material portion of FTX transfers to CFAR was used to fund Lightcone and the acquisition and renovation of the inn. The same source says a hotel at that address was bought 'in part' with FTX Foundation funds. It also says the complaint described the $1M as intended as a loan. A Substack excerpt gives the same account (https://davidzmorris.substack.com/p/a-lever-long-enough-draft-excerpt).

The claim has four problems:
- The purchaser was Lightcone RG, a CFAR subsidiary, and the money was wired to a title company, not to CFAR itself.
- The funding was only partial. Lightcone said the Rose Garden Inn was bought on a loan from Jaan Tallinn, about $16M, and that it had other funders such as Open Phil and SFF (https://forum.effectivealtruism.org/posts/rsnrpvKofps5Py7di/shutting-down-the-lightcone-offices).
- The payments came in July and August 2022, before FTX collapsed in November 2022. 'As it was collapsing' is loose, though the estate suit argues the payments were made when insiders knew FTX was fragile.
- The FTX estate's complaint is an allegation. CFAR contested the clawback.

Overall the claim is broadly supported but simplified, since 'originally purchased with money wired to CFAR' overstates how much of the purchase FTX paid for.

The safety, red team and alignment teams seem especially afflicted, because that's the area you go on to worry about and try to work against AI doom, which you are sure is at least medium likely. cascade.findings: The claim captures a real EA concept but overstates it as a universal creed-prescription. Effective altruism does promote "earning to give," defined as "choosing a high-paying career so that you can donate a large percentage of your income to charity, for example, by working as a financial trader, a software engineer, or a management consultant" https://www.centreforeffectivealtruism.org/effective-altruism-sam-bankman-fried and "whereby someone seeks out a high-paying career in order to donate a substantial portion of that income to particularly impactful charities" https://www.givingwhatwecan.org/misconceptions-and-concerns-about-effective-altruism-and-charity-evaluation . However EA sources explicitly reject that this is a creed-wide requirement: "effective altruism is a project rather than an ideology or set of assumptions/answers" with "no one right way" and "how can we do the most good with our limited time and resources?" as central question https://www.givingwhatwecan.org/misconceptions-and-concerns-about-effective-altruism-and-charity-evaluation ; "Media coverage often mistakenly equates effective altruism entirely with this one path even though only some people within the community take this route", and 80,000 Hours "believes earning to give is only right for 'a small proportion of people'" https://www.givingwhatwecan.org/misconceptions-and-concerns-about-effective-altruism-and-charity-evaluation . 80,000 Hours further argues the community put "too much weight on earning to give and fundraising" and should focus more on talent/direct work https://80000hours.org/2015/11/why-you-should-focus-more-on-talent-gaps-not-funding-gaps/ , where "Earning to give (taking a higher earning career and donating the extra money to high-impact charities) is the most distinctive career path" but not the only model. Therefore describing finance-seeking to donate as EA creed prescribes is misleading by universalizing an optional, minority, and increasingly de-emphasised strategy.

EA's stated core is impartial maximising of good, cause prioritization and cost-effectiveness, with varied career paths including direct research, policy and nonprofit work https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Effective_altruism . The article's phrasing 'by creed, says you should' therefore overstates universality, but as an explanation for why some EAs go into finance to give more, it captures a real, promoted doctrine.

## Research findings

The claim is misleading. It is partly grounded in Yudkowsky's text, but 'acts of terrorism' and 'euphemism' go beyond what he wrote.

What Yudkowsky defined:
- Arbital defines 'pivotal act' as a 'guarded term' for actions that make a large positive difference a billion years later (https://arbital.greaterwrong.com/p/pivotal/). It is a technical term for decisive, positive, gameboard-changing events. It is not specifically a term for violence.
- AISafety.info says that under Yudkowsky's definition a pivotal act involves powerful AI. It adds that a human attack on a single AI lab would not count under his definition (https://aisafety.info/questions/7580/).
- One commentary says a pivotal act need not involve taking over the world (https://www.greaterwrong.com/posts/MtkcDDf2ZPvFk4jtN/pivotal-acts-might-not-be-what-you-think-they-are). Its author argues that creating a powerful global institution that effectively regulates AI could count. This is a secondary source, not Yudkowsky's own wording.

What the claim gets right:
- In 'AGI Ruin: A List of Lethalities', Yudkowsky says that while few actors have AGI, they 'must execute some pivotal act', one strong enough to flip the gameboard. He also says all known pivotal acts are outside the Overton Window (https://www.greaterwrong.com/posts/uMQ3cqWDPHhjtiesc/agi-ruin-a-list-of-lethalities).
- His example is 'burn all GPUs'. The act is meant to stop others from building unaligned AGI, so it is coercive and unilateral. Critics call such acts a coup or a suppression of humanity (https://lironshapira.substack.com/p/holly-elmore-case-against-eliezer, https://www.lesswrong.com/posts/JFNjbMXpJYqvgasaK/we-should-think-about-the-pivotal-act-again-here-s-a-better).

- Yudkowsky says he does not actually advocate burning all GPUs. He calls it a 'mild overestimate' of the power level needed, and says it is not what he would actually want a powerful AGI to do (https://www.greaterwrong.com/posts/uMQ3cqWDPHhjtiesc/agi-ruin-a-list-of-lethalities).
- The acts are framed as performed by an aligned AGI. They are not described as terrorist acts by 'anyone making AGI'. Calling them terrorism is the critic's own loaded label, not Yudkowsky's.
- Calling the term a 'euphemism' is the author's interpretation. Arbital explicitly describes it as a 'guarded' technical term.
- I did not re-fetch the 2023 TIME op-ed. My earlier point that it called for treaties and state enforcement against rogue datacenters is from memory and is not source-backed here.

cascade.findings: Yudkowsky defines a 'pivotal act' as preventing others from building unaligned AGI: "We need to align the performance of some large task, a 'pivotal act' that prevents other people from building an unaligned AGI that destroys the world. While the number of actors with AGI is few or one, they must execute some 'pivotal act', strong enough to flip the gameboard, using an AGI powerful enough to do that" https://intelligence.org/2022/06/10/agi-ruin/ . His stock example is "burn all GPUs" https://intelligence.org/2022/06/10/agi-ruin/ , elsewhere described as melting all GPUs globally or subtly changing GPUs so they can't be used for AGI https://forum.nunosempere.com/s/crosspost-ai-regulation-may-be-more-important-than-ai-alignment-for-existential-safety , and as nanomachines that hunt down and burn all GPUs https://manifold.markets/question/is-there-a-pivotal-weak-act . He explicitly acknowledges "all known pivotal acts are currently outside the Overton Window" https://intelligence.org/2022/06/10/agi-ruin/ . Crucially the act is framed as performed by/using a powerful aligned AGI, not as human builders personally committing violence, and summaries stress "to avoid catastrophe, whoever builds AGI first will have to a) align it... c) do some pivotal act that prevents others from scaling it up" https://lesswrong.com/posts/f4c5BUSfip之类 — i.e. first/few actors, conditional, via AGI. In his 2023 TIME moratorium proposal he advocated state action: participating countries should be willing to take military action such as "destroy[ing] a rogue datacenter by airstrike" to enforce a moratorium https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eliezer_Yudkowsky . That is described as interstate military force / enforcement of international agreements, not non-state terrorism, and other descriptions of pivotal-act proposals include "establish unbreakable international agreements, or develop other mechanisms that make uncontrolled AI development physically impossible" https://github.com/centresecuriteia/aisafety_atlas_multilingual/blob/main/docs/chapters/03/10.md . Calling the whole category "acts of terrorism" that "anyone making AGI must do" therefore conflates AGI-executed disabling of compute and state-enforced moratorium with terrorism, overgeneralizes "first/few under time-limit competition" to "anyone," and treats an openly-discussed extreme-power requirement as a euphemistic cover.

cascade.findings:
Yudkowsky does define a 'pivotal act' as a large task that a first/early aligned AGI-builder must perform to stop others building unaligned AGI that destroys the world: "We need to align the performance of some large task, a 'pivotal act' that prevents other people from building an unaligned AGI that destroys the world. While the number of actors with AGI is few or one, they must execute some 'pivotal act', strong enough to flip the gameboard, using an AGI powerful enough to do that." His illustrative example is "burn all GPUs" https://intelligence.org/2022/06/10/agi-ruin/ - summarized elsewhere as preventing other actors from building unaligned AGI that kills all humans, e.g. "Releasing nanomachines that hunt down and burn all GPUs is a 'pivotal act'" https://manifold.markets etc., and as "something you can get the aligned superintelligent AI to do to prevent any other labs from building unaligned AI" https://www.lesswrong.com/posts/Lpurs5qXDG8irSDXm/is-ai-alignment-enough . That supports the "must do under certain circumstances to prevent competition/end of world" part.

Calling it "acts of terrorism" is inflammatory/misleading: Yudkowsky frames it as an AI-performed strategic/technological intervention (disabling compute, e.g. melt/burn GPUs, establish agreements, make uncontrolled development physically impossible https://github.com/centresecuriteia/aisafety_atlas_multilingual/blob/main/docs/chapters/03/10.md ), not unlawful anti-civilian violence for political intimidation. His separate human-enforcement proposal was for states to enforce a moratorium, including "be willing to destroy a rogue datacenter by airstrike" https://www.businessinsider.mx etc., reported as "In his notorious TIME op-ed, 'Shut it All Down,' he argued that governments should 'be willing to destroy a rogue datacenter by airstrike.'" https://www.techdirt.com/2025/08/15/the-ai-docs-falsehoods-and-false-balance/ - state military action, not "terrorism," and conditional on violating a global shutdown/moratorium, not an unconditional duty of "anyone making AGI." Yudkowsky explicitly says burn-all-GPUs is "not what I think you'd actually want to do" but "a mild overestimate for the rough power level" https://intelligence.org/2022/06/10/agi-ruin/ , undermining "euphemism for terrorism" claim.

Text from Article: Allegedly, Effective Altruism and its AI safety efforts are a separate thing and not directly beholden to Yudkowsky. This is fundamentally not true. Effective Altruism in the Bay Area has almost perfect overlap with rationalism, and the Effective Altruist AI Safety people in the Bay set the agenda for the rest of Effective Altruism’s safety efforts.
Claim: Effective Altruism and its AI safety efforts are directly beholden to Eliezer Yudkowsky rather than separate from him.

## Research findings

The claim overstates the relationship. Yudkowsky's influence on EA AI safety is real, but EA's AI safety work is not directly beholden to him.

Evidence of influence and overlap:
- MIRI, which Yudkowsky co-founded, is described as the original AI safety technical research organization (https://www.aipanic.news/p/the-ai-existential-risk-industrial). Open Philanthropy gave it grants of about $14M (https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/03085147.2024.2439715).
- An EA Forum commenter says MIRI's intellectual DNA contains much of Yudkowsky's thought (https://forum.effectivealtruism.org/posts/rhidnFTcWufnzypfh/how-effective-and-efficient-is-the-funding-policy-of-open).
- Luke Muehlhauser, a former MIRI executive director, later oversaw Open Philanthropy's AI risk program (https://www.aipanic.news/p/effective-altruism-funded-the-ai). This is a personal link, not control.

Evidence against 'directly beholden':
- Open Philanthropy was skeptical of MIRI for years. Holden Karnofsky declined to recommend a MIRI grant even though he agreed with many of MIRI's controversial views. Open Phil revised that decision in 2015 (https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/03085147.2024.2439715).
- Open Phil had twelve anonymous reviewers assess MIRI papers. The reviewers were critical of the work, and MIRI itself said it was more confident than the reviewers (https://intelligence.org/2016/09/06/grant-open-philanthropy/, https://intelligence.org/files/OpenPhil2016Supplement.pdf).
- Open Phil's AI safety money went to many other groups. Between 2016 and 2023, over $270M went to AI safety research, including $30M to OpenAI and $211M to CHAI at UC Berkeley. MIRI received only $14M (https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/03085147.2024.2439715). RAND and FAR AI also received large grants (https://www.aipanic.news/p/the-ai-existential-risk-industrial).
- Some AI safety organizations explicitly distance themselves from EA. The Center for AI Safety said it has not taken Open Phil funding for years and that AI safety has outgrown the EA community (https://x.com/CAIS/status/2034389842076025164). This also shows AI safety is not a single EA-run effort.

I did not find a source on the Bay Area EA-rationalist overlap beyond general context, so I give no source for that part.

Verdict: 'Influence and overlap' is defensible. 'Directly beholden' is a polemical overstatement.

## Research findings

The claim is an overstated opinion. EA and Yudkowsky's rationalist community overlap and influence each other heavily. The sources I found do not show that EA or its AI-safety efforts are 'directly beholden' to him.

Support for overlap and influence:
- Wikipedia's page on the rationalist community lists effective altruism and AI safety (specifically AI extinction risk) among 'heavily overlapping communities'. It also says the community's borders are blurry and debated. That fits 'heavy overlap' but not 'almost perfect' or identical. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rationalist_community
- An EA Forum piece says effective altruists are heavily influenced by the rationalist community. That community formed around Yudkowsky's Sequences, and it has shaped how EAs reason. https://forum.effectivealtruism.org/posts/KCinzpuWgaEcSYPJ8/rationalist-epistemics-and-the-sequences-effective-altruism
- Yudkowsky founded LessWrong in 2009, seeding it with his Overcoming Bias posts. https://forum.effectivealtruism.org/topics/lesswrong
- A community discussion (a forum thread, so weak evidence) says EA combined several groups: Giving What We Can, 80,000 Hours, GiveWell and MIRI. It says rationalists were a major early source of recruits, and that most recruiting is now independent of rationalists. https://awful.systems/post/631639
- A critical overview says EA's institutional center shifted toward AI safety and that this aligned with the rationalist community's interests. It says the two communities, with longtermism, converged into one social network. https://garden.johanneskleske.com/effective-altruism

Evidence against 'directly beholden':
- Open Philanthropy (now Coefficient Giving), the largest funder in existential-risk reduction, runs open technical AI-safety grant programs. These fund academics, nonprofits and independent researchers, with about $40M committed in 2025. https://grantedai.com/grants/open-philanthropy-request-for-proposals-technical-ai-safety-coefficient-giving-formerly-open-philant-809e59b7
- An Ohio State news item shows an academic engineering professor receiving Open Philanthropy AI-safety grants. This shows the field extends well beyond Yudkowsky's circle. https://engineering.osu.edu/news/2025/09/ai-safety-research-attracts-funding-open-philanthropy
- The same thread notes EA's origins in several groups, not only Yudkowsky's. These include GiveWell, Giving What We Can and 80,000 Hours. https://awful.systems/post/631639

I could not verify from fetched pages that many EA AI-safety researchers disagree with Yudkowsky. That is background knowledge only, so I have not relied on it.

Conclusion: the influence and overlap are real. 'Directly beholden' and 'almost perfect overlap' overstate it, because EA has multiple origins, funders and organizations.

## Research findings

Eliezer Yudkowsky has no formal academic degree. He is a self-taught researcher who co-founded the Machine Intelligence Research Institute (MIRI), originally the Singularity Institute, in 2000. He is known for foundational work on AI alignment, including "friendly AI" and decision theory papers, some of them published as technical reports and in volumes. He also wrote popular works such as HPMOR, the Sequences, and the 2025 book "If Anyone Builds It, Everyone Dies". Describing him as a writer is partly accurate. Saying he is "not a scientist of any kind" is contestable. He is an AI safety researcher and theorist, but he has no PhD, few peer-reviewed publications, and no empirical lab science. Whether he counts as a scientist depends on the definition. The claim is a framing used to discredit him, and it is arguably an oversimplification. It is not clearly false. cascade.findings: The first half is true – Yudkowsky is a writer/author. The second half – “and not a scientist [of any kind]” – is misleading. Mainstream biographical sources describe him as BOTH researcher/scientist AND writer: Wikipedia defines him as “an American artificial intelligence researcher and writer on decision theory and ethics” who “is the founder of and a research fellow at the Machine Intelligence Research Institute (MIRI)” https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eliezer_Yudkowsky . TED lists him as “founder and research fellow at the Machine Intelligence Research Institute” with “more than 20 years of experience in the world of artificial intelligence” https://www.ted.com/speakers/eliezer_yudkowsky . Edge.org lists “ELIEZER YUDKOWSKY is a research fellow of the Machine Intelligence Research Institute, which he co-founded in 2001” https://www.edge.org/memberbio/eliezer_s_yudkowsky . Other bios call him “an American artificial intelligence researcher, writer, and decision theorist recognized as a founding figure in the field of AI alignment” https://www.allamericanspeakers.com/speakers/465431/Eliezer-Yudkowsky , and “a decision theorist, computer scientist, and author who co-founded and leads research at the Machine Intelligence Research Institute” https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=some-robinson-podcast and Sam Harris site “a decision theorist and computer scientist at the Machine Intelligence Research Institute” https://samharris.org/guests/eliezer-yudkowsky . Publisher bio calls him “a founding researcher of the field of AI alignment, with influential work spanning more than twenty years” https://www.amazon.com/Anyone-Builds-Everyone-Dies-Superhuman/dp/0316595642 . He is author of Rationality: From AI to Zombies, Harry Potter and the Methods of Rationality, and co-author of NYT bestseller If Anyone Builds It, Everyone Dies https://books.theunseen.city/library/eliezer-yudkowsky . It is true he lacks formal credentials – he “did not attend high school or college” and is self-taught/autodidact https://klu.ai/blog/who-is-eliezer-yudkowsky , but that does not make “not a scientist of any kind” accurate given 20+ years as a full-time research fellow whose work influenced Nick Bostrom’s Superintelligence and mainstream AI risk research.

cascade.findings: Claim is well-supported by labor history sources and is not misleading. The AFL was founded in 1886 as a loose federation of craft unions under Samuel Gompers, dedicated to principles of craft unionism https://www.britannica.com/topic/AFL-CIO . Its approximately 100 national and international unions retained full autonomy and each received "exclusive jurisdiction" over a craft, with "one union per craft; one craft per union," which produced bitter jurisdictional disputes between affiliates https://www.britannica.com/topic/AFL-CIO . Craft unions are described as organizing by specific craft/trade (e.g., all carpenters in carpenters' union, plasterers in plasterers' union) with own administration, agreements and halls https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Craft_unionism . Coming out of guild tradition, they policed how work was done by "maintaining standards for admission into the trade; requiring entrants to go through an apprenticeship program controlled by the union, rather than the employer; and dictating the processes, tools, standards, and pace of work" https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Craft_unionism . Related summaries note membership was exclusive to those with particular skills to maintain strong control over labor supply in specialized areas, limiting membership to skilled workers and excluding unskilled workers, with craft exclusivity creating barriers to entry https://www.britannica.com/topic/AFL-CIO https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Craft_unionism . AFL unions required union members only via closed shop and "Selective admission to apprenticeships restricted membership, thereby artificially limiting the supply of skilled labor" is the standard textbook description of early trade-union control.

cascade.findings: Claim is directionally true as a first-order expectation (if per-ask acceptance probability p is constant, expected dates = n*p), but "approximately linear" overstates precision and ignores documented non-linearities. Average match-to-date conversion is only 10-15%, with 60-70% of matches never exchanging messages and users needing 50-100 matches to secure one actual date https://checklovers.com/blog/dating-statistics/online-dating-success-rate-statistics - more attempts do yield more dates on average, supporting monotonicity. However: 1) Selectivity improves outcomes - being slightly pickier (30-50% swipe-right rate) leads to better match quality and conversation rates than swiping right on everyone, contradicting simple "lower standards = proportionally more dates" https://checklovers.com/blog/dating-statistics/online-dating-success-rate-statistics . 2) More matches don't necessarily mean more success - women receive 5-10x more matches than men but converting attention into quality dates is just as challenging https://checklovers.com/blog/dating-statistics/online-dating-success-rate-statistics . 3) Rejection mind-set experiments show acceptance chance falls on average 27% from first to last partner option, explained by decline in satisfaction with pictures and perceived dating success, with people gradually "closing off" from opportunities https://www.researchgate.net/publication/335312368_A_Rejection_Mind-Set_Choice_Overload_in_Online_Dating . 4) Logic of diminishing returns: being presented with the 250th option does not add as much benefit as the 12th, leading to decreased satisfaction, increased regret, decision complexity and cognitive load https://abcwest.sitehost.iu.edu/pmwiki/pdf/lenton.shoppingcart.2010.pdf . Average ROI is also poor (90 minutes daily for ~one date per month) with burnout/paradox of choice https://checklovers.com/blog/dating-statistics/online-dating-success-rate-statistics . So linearity is a rough heuristic, not an empirical scaling law; returns diminish with volume/effort.

## Research findings

Rovell's tweet compares two different and incompatible statistics. For the 2026 Finals, multiple outlets confirm Game 5 of the Knicks-Spurs series averaged 24.5 million viewers and peaked at 33 million late in the telecast as the Knicks rallied to win (https://variety.com/2026/tv/ratings/knicks-nba-championship-game-ratings-1236783260/, https://www.nba.com/news/nba-finals-2026-viewership-most-watched-28-years). 33 million is a simultaneous, average-minute peak audience figure. Dividing by the current U.S. population (~346M) yields almost exactly 9.5%, matching Rovell's number.

For the 1998 Bulls-Jazz Game 6, Wikipedia's list of NBA Finals ratings states the game averaged a 22.3 rating/38 share and 35.89 million viewers, making it the highest-rated and most-watched NBA game on record (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NBA_Finals_television_ratings). However, the 1998 NBA playoffs Wikipedia page separately notes it was the highest rated and most watched game in NBA history, with 72 million viewers watching at least part of the game and an average of 35.9 million viewers (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1998_NBA_playoffs). Contemporary reporting from the Washington Post confirms NBC estimated that 72 million people watched all or part of the game, a figure based on cumulative reach across the whole broadcast, not a simultaneous peak (https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/lifestyle/1998/06/17/bulls-a-winner-for-nbc/9e4ac4dd-ecb0-4aa8-b6fd-a6f6e56535a6/). 72 million divided by the roughly 276 million U.S. population in 1998 comes out to about 26.1%, matching Rovell's cited figure precisely — meaning he used the 'watched any portion' cumulative reach number for 1998, not a comparable simultaneous peak.

This is an apples-to-oranges comparison: Rovell pairs the 2026 game's simultaneous peak-minute audience (33M) against the 1998 game's cumulative total reach across the whole broadcast (72M watched at least part of the game). Cumulative reach is always substantially larger than any single-minute peak, so using it for 1998 while using true peak for 2026 inflates the apparent gap between the two eras. If both were calculated the same way — e.g., comparing average viewership, where 1998 drew 35.89 million (about 13% of the 1998 population) against 2026's average of 24.5 million for Game 5 or 20.6 million for the series (about 6-7% of today's population) — the disparity implied would look notably different from the 26.1% vs 9.5% framing in the tweet, though 1998 would still be clearly higher either way. Separately, all sources agree the 2026 Knicks-Spurs series was the most-watched NBA Finals since 1998, averaging 20.6 million viewers across the five games (https://www.nba.com/news/nba-finals-2026-viewership-most-watched-28-years), so the broader point that 1998 drew a proportionally far larger audience is directionally correct, but the specific percentages Rovell cites conflate incompatible metrics (peak audience vs. cumulative total reach), which could mislead readers about the actual scale of the viewership gap.

For the 2026 Finals, multiple outlets confirm Game 5 of the Knicks-Spurs series averaged 24.5 million viewers and peaked at 33 million late in the telecast as the Knicks rallied to win (https://variety.com/2026/tv/ratings/knicks-nba-championship-game-ratings-1236783260/, https://www.nba.com/news/nba-finals-2026-viewership-most-watched-28-years). 33 million is a simultaneous, average-minute peak audience figure. Dividing by the current U.S. population (~346M) yields almost exactly 9.5%, matching Rovell's number.

For the 1998 Bulls-Jazz Game 6, Wikipedia's list of NBA Finals ratings states the game averaged a 22.3 rating/38 share and 35.89 million viewers, making it the highest-rated and most-watched NBA game on record (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NBA_Finals_television_ratings). However, the 1998 NBA playoffs Wikipedia page separately notes it was the highest rated and most watched game in NBA history, with 72 million viewers watching at least part of the game and an average of 35.9 million viewers (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1998_NBA_playoffs). Cumulative reach is always substantially larger than any single-minute peak, so using it for 1998 while using true peak for 2026 inflates the apparent gap between the two eras. ## Research findings

Post claims Steam enforces its own DRM on all games, requires login every 30 days to reauthenticate, and games break 30 days after Steam goes down. This is misleading/false. Steam's DRM wrapper (Custom Executable Generation/CEG) is optional and developer-applied, not platform-enforced - Valve docs describe it as a tool developers choose to apply via SteamPipe/drm_wrap or App Admin Security Tab https://partner.steamgames.com/doc/features/drm - third-party docs describe it as "an optional extra tool you can use when you have sent builds to the store" https://help.yoyogames.com/hc/en-us/articles/13551041141841-Steamworks-SDK-Setting-Up-Your-Games and PCGamingWiki maintains a large list of DRM-free games on Steam that work without Steam client https://pcgamingwiki.com/wiki/The_big_list_of_DRM-free_games_on_Steam - supporting quoted post that DRM is developer/publisher decision. No 30-day reauth exists: Valve programmer Henry Goffin stated "Offline Mode is designed to be indefinite... the client should allow you to run in Offline Mode for as long as you like" https://www.pcgamesn.com/steam-offline-mode-designed-be-indefinite-valve-are-working-make-it-more-robust - directly rebutting a "two week" reset claim. Nuance: some individual games add third-party DRM (e.g. Denuvo) that may require periodic online checks, and Steam offline has had bugs, but that is not a Steam-enforced 30-day license check. GOG installers being DRM-free/forever is broadly correct.

samples.research:
The tweet claims Steam itself enforces DRM via mandatory 30-day reauthentication, such that 'your games will break in 30 days once Steam goes down,' contrasted with GOG backups working forever. This claim is contested and partially misleading.

Supporting the tweet's premise: Many users report time-limited offline mode. A 2013 Steam forum user reported "So there is some sort of time limited DRM on steam offline mode, and it will stop working after about 2 weeks" (https://steamcommunity.com/discussions/forum/1/828937979095845728). Another forum thread describes "The Steam Offline Mode requires being re-logged in and validated on a regular basis (something like once every 30 days or so), you cant just set it offline and be good, it will eventualy fail and require re-authentication" (https://steamcommunity.com/discussions/forum/0/1700542332330146872). Current guides (2026) similarly state users can typically play "approximately 14 to 30 days before the client requires a re-authentication handshake" (https://gamewiki.blog/what-happens-if-i-play-steam-games-offline).

However, Valve's own official position directly contradicts the tweet's framing that this is Steam enforcing DRM by design. A Valve employee stated on the Steam forums: "This is not actually true - Offline Mode is designed to be indefinite... That said, there are many components involved in Offline Mode, and some of them have known issues and bugs which we are continually working to improve... It is not broken 'by design.'" and noted "The 'two week' timeout issue has been fixed for months now, along with several other bugs" (https://steamcommunity.com/discussions/forum/1/864969953572102601). This was also reported by Blue's News: "A response from Valve to a thread about offline mode on Steam indicates that the way offline mode currently requires users to go online periodically... is a bug, and not working as intended" (https://www.bluesnews.com/cgi-bin/board.pl?action=viewthread&boardid=1&threadid=146408).

Crucially, much of the real-world lockout behavior users experience is attributable to third-party DRM (especially Denuvo) layered onto specific games by publishers, not Steam's core platform. One forum user explained: "If you have games with Denuvo or other DRM, of launchers, they will ask to phone home every period (like 30 days)" (https://steamcommunity.com/discussions/forum/0/587308261888419215/). Another user directly addressed the 'Steam is secretly like Denuvo' argument: "There isn't any compulsory DRM in Steam. It's the publisher/developer's choice whether they want to implement it or not... it allows to play offline indefinitely and backup and reinstall your whole library at will while offline at all times" and added "All games using Valve's DRM allow offline play indefinitely since 2013" (https://steamcommunity.com/app/359870/discussions/0/1850323802590261402). A 2026 Notebookcheck report confirms Denuvo (third-party), not Steam, is tightening restrictions: "A hypervisor bypass developer discovered Denuvo now asks players to authenticate tokens online every 14 days" and "Many Steam games, besides NBA 2K26, already penalize offline players" due to Denuvo specifically (https://www.notebookcheck.net/Denuvo-bolsters-DRM-in-Steam-games-even-as-hypervisor-achieves-piracy-milestone.1283939.0.html).

Also, Valve's Steamworks DRM (when publishers opt in) is distinguishable from third-party DRM like Denuvo, and developers can use Steamworks services without enabling Steam's own DRM at all, undercutting the tweet's claim that Steam 'enforces their own DRM' universally.

In short: the empirical behavior many users observe (games failing after ~2-4 weeks offline) is real and documented, but it is predominantly driven by third-party DRM (Denuvo) that publishers choose to add, exactly as the quoted post states ('If a game has DRM, that is a developer/publisher decision'). Valve has stated Steam's own offline mode is designed/intended to be indefinite, contradicting the tweet's framing that Steam itself mandates a 30-day reauthentication that will inevitably break all games. The tweet overgeneralizes a real but inconsistent, largely third-party-DRM-driven phenomenon as an official, universal Steam-enforced 30-day DRM rule, which misrepresents the distinction the quoted post was making.

cascade.findings: Post claims Steam enforces its own DRM, requires login every 30 days to reauthenticate, and games will break in 30 days if Steam goes down, vs GOG installers work forever. This is misleading on first two points: Steam DRM wrapper / CEG is optional and applied by developer choice, not enforced by Steam on all games - Valve docs describe DRM wrap as a tool developers run via drm_wrap / App Admin Security Tab to add DRM to your exe https://partner.steamgames.com/doc/features/drm . Third-party docs describe it as "optional extra tool you can use" https://help.yoyogames.com/hc/en-us/articles/115001434911-Steamworks-SDK-Setting-Up-Your-Games and PCGamingWiki states "Steamworks DRM is called Custom Executable Generation (CEG) and like every part of Steamworks, it's optional for the developers. There are many games which use Steamworks and are DRM-free." https://www.pcgamingwiki.com/wiki/The_big_list_of_DRM-free_games_on_Steam - supported by existence of large list of DRM-free games on Steam https://www.pcgamingwiki.com/wiki/The_big_list_of_DRM-free_games_on_Steam . Quoted post that DRM is developer/publisher decision is therefore correct. 30-day re-auth claim is false per Valve: Valve programmer Henry Goffin / HenryG stated "Offline Mode is designed to be indefinite... the client should allow you to run in Offline Mode for as long as you like" https://steamcommunity.com/discussions/forum/1/864969953572102601/#c864969953730401285 , reported at https://www.pcgamesn.com/steam-offline-mode-designed-to-be-indefinite and https://www.eurogamer.net/valve-working-to-make-offline-mode-indefinite and https://www.pcgamer.com/steam-client-should-allow-you-to-run-in-offline-mode-for-as-long-as-you-like-say-valve/ and https://www.cinemablend.com/games/Steam-Offline-Mode-Designed-Indefinite-Says-Valve-69859.html and https://kotaku.com/valve-is-constantly-trying-to-improve-steams-wonky-off-1722154720 . No 30-day limit in official docs; confusion may come from old 2-week bug Valve said was not intended. Nuance: games that DO use Steam DRM wrapper do require Steam client to launch to verify ownership https://partner.steamgames.com/doc/features/drm , so if Steam permanently disappeared without patch, those titles would need removal of wrapper / crack, while DRM-free titles on Steam would continue to launch directly; GOG offline installers part is broadly true.

In the US involuntary hospitalization does not cancel debts and patients still owe for care: 'the patient is generally responsible for the cost, just as with any other hospital stay' https://legalclarity.org/maryland-involuntary-commitment-laws-and-procedures-explained/ . In South Africa (author location) the National Credit Act provides debt counselling / debt review as negotiation for reduced payments and restructured plans, not cancellation: 'Debt counselling was introduced in 2007, through the National Credit Act, as a debt relief measure' and 'having a registered debt counsellor negotiate with creditors on your behalf for reduced payments (in line with your disposable income), as well as putting forth restructured payment plans – which are referred to court for final determination' https://www.iolnews.co.za/personal-finance/debt/indebted-south-africans-waking-up-to-the-benefits-of-debt-counselling-ad90a1ea-3f6c-4f96-afc1-e9f8ded7be6a and the same source says clearance requires repayment: 'They are fully aware that while under debt review, they will not have access to new credit, as the goal is to first clean their slate of existing debt' and 'access to credit will only change once they have settled all their short term debt and their payments on their mortgage agreements are up to date. Only when all of these conditions have been satisfied, can their debt counsellor issue them with a clearance certificate' https://www.iolnews.co.za/personal-finance/debt/indebted-south-africans-waking-up-to-the-benefits-of-debt-counselling-ad90a1ea-3f6c-4f96-afc1-e9f8ded7be6a .

In the US, involuntary hospitalization does NOT cancel debts; patients/guardians remain liable for costs of commitment and care, with no provision for free private-facility involuntary care https://myfloridalegal.com/ and hospitals evaluate medical/financial/legal situation but care must be paid for https://www.answer-all.com/ and https://casetext.com/ . Narrow exception is US federal student loan Total and Permanent Disability Discharge, which requires physician certification of inability to engage in substantial gainful activity due to mental/physical impairment lasting 60+ months / expected 60+ months or death https://lanterncredit.com/ and under Higher Education Act only death or total/permanent disability qualifies https://www.shepherdelderlaw.com/ - not mere psychiatric hold. In South Africa (author location), National Credit Act 34 of 2005 provides only debt counselling / restructuring, not cancellation on institutionalization https://www.meerkat.co.za/ and https://moneyweb.co.za/ . Hospital charity care may reduce/eliminate that hospital's bill based on income https://www.goodrx.com/ but does not cancel all other debts.

The Daily Wire tweet retells the viral 'Oreogate' saga—a mom who asked other parents to stop packing Oreos, emailed the school, and allegedly searched another child's lunchbox, prompting other moms to organize an 'Oreo Day' in retaliation. The plot details match the viral Instagram narrative widely reported across outlets like Today's Parent and Stomp.sg describing the lunchbox search and the coordinated retaliation by other mothers.

Critically, the Daily Wire presents this as a straightforward factual news story with no indication that it is widely suspected to be fabricated/staged advertising content. Investigative reporting from Business Insider found that the Instagram account 'ashleighjamz,' which created the viral 'Oreogate' video series, is a paid creator partner for Suno, an AI music generator, with every installment tagged #sunopartner and turned into an AI-generated song (https://x.com/katienotopoulos/status/2093413624165343436). Suno confirmed to Business Insider it was a paid partnership, and Oreo's manufacturer Mondelez denied any involvement (https://www.mediaweek.com.au/oreogate-viral-lunchbox-row-suno-ad-controversy). The creator, Ashleigh Jamz, repeatedly declined to confirm whether the messages, parents, and events depicted were real, according to Business Insider's investigation as reported by https://www.dexerto.com/food/viral-oreogate-mom-drama-was-a-paid-ai-ad-and-its-creator-wont-say-if-it-was-real-3403588/. Media commentary (SheKnows) noted the account was less than a month old and consisted solely of similar dramatized, monetized storylines, with commenters arguing anyone treating the posts as real lacks media literacy (https://www.sheknows.com/parenting/articles/1235074192/moms-oreos-was-it-fake/).

As of current reporting, there is no definitive confirmation the events were entirely fabricated, but there is also no confirmation they were real — it remains officially unresolved, though widely suspected to be scripted/staged ad content tied to an undisclosed or semi-disclosed influencer marketing campaign (https://www.mediaweek.com.au/oreogate-viral-lunchbox-row-suno-ad-controversy).

The Daily Wire tweet presents this story with no acknowledgment of its disputed, likely-fabricated nature, framing it as if it were a real, organic news event. This omission is the kind of missing context that would benefit from a Community Note, since multiple credible outlets (Business Insider, SheKnows, Dexerto, Mediaweek) have reported this is very likely an AI-generated, paid advertising campaign for Suno rather than an authentic parenting dispute.

The Daily Wire's tweet retells 'Oreogate' as a straightforward, factual account of a real parenting dispute: a mom asked other parents to ban Oreos, the school refused, the teacher refused, so she searched another child's lunchbox, prompting the group chat to retaliate with 'Oreo Day.' However, the entire 'Oreogate' saga has been widely reported as likely fake/fabricated advertising content, not a real event. It originated solely from a single Instagram account, @ashleighjamz, which posted screenshots of an alleged group chat set to AI-generated songs as part of a paid partnership with AI music company Suno (https://www.dexerto.com/food/viral-oreogate-mom-drama-was-a-paid-ai-ad-and-its-creator-wont-say-if-it-was-real-3403588/). Suno confirmed 'that @ashleighjamz is one of its paid creator partners' though it said it 'did not devise or control the Oreogate storyline' (https://tigerjek.com/viral-oreogate-mom-drama-was-a-paid-ai-ad-and-its-creator-wont-say-if-it-was-real/). Crucially, when asked directly whether the events were real, 'ashleighjamz did not directly answer when asked whether the messages, parents and children featured in Oreogate were real' and stopped responding to further questions (https://www.dexerto.com/food/viral-oreogate-mom-drama-was-a-paid-ai-ad-and-its-creator-wont-say-if-it-was-real-3403588/).

Journalists flagged major red flags: the account 'was created less than a month' before the saga and 'consists solely of Suno-related posts in the same format,' depicting other 'dramas' like workplace and bachelorette-party fights, all set to AI-generated songs (https://www.yahoo.com/lifestyle/family-relationships/article/a-mom-complained-about-her-daughters-classmate-bringing-cookies-to-school-welcome-to-oreo-gate-214328869.html). A viral tweet from a social-media expert noted '“oreogate” is just fake storytime ads from the company suno but it's being reported as real by the media' (https://x.com/milkkarten/status/2093057849656324598). Local news coverage flagged: 'There is some talk online that "Oreogate" may not have been a real mom-group meltdown at all. The posts have not been verified as actual conversations, and the music playing was reportedly generated by AI' (https://mynorthwest.com/kiro-radio/oreogate-parents/4277575). Oreo itself publicly distanced itself from the story, and commentary pieces outright state 'Oreogate Is Probably Fake' (https://www.purewow.com/family/oreogate-mom-group-chat-debate). As of the latest reporting, 'There is currently no confirmation that the Oreogate messages were fabricated,' but equally no confirmation they were real, and the creator's refusal to clarify combined with the account's ad-only history strongly suggests this was manufactured content rather than a genuine news event (https://tigerjek.com/viral-oreogate-mom-drama-was-a-paid-ai-ad-and-its-creator-wont-say-if-it-was-real/).

The Daily Wire's tweet presents this as a real-world event with no indication it may be AI-generated/sponsored fictional content, which is misleading given the substantial evidence and widespread reporting questioning its authenticity.

## Research findings

The claim in the tweet ('cornrows were used by runaway slaves to map escape routes, as well as store food for their journey') is a widely-circulated piece of internet folklore that fact-checkers have examined extensively and found lacks solid historical documentation. Snopes investigated this claim twice (2022 and 2026) and concluded: 'We read a number of accounts, and found no tangible evidence of slaves in the U.S. actually using cornrows to convey messages' (https://www.snopes.com/news/2022/03/12/maps-cornrows-black-slaves-escape/, https://www.snopes.com/news/2026/05/16/slaves-braided-maps-cornrows/). Snopes describes it as 'kind of urban legends that [serve a] function of giving particulars to generalities' rather than a verified historical fact, quoting a folklore historian who noted the story 'make[s] concrete [or] give[s] a story to something that is ultimately very true' in spirit but not necessarily in documented fact.

The most-cited historical basis for the legend is specific to Colombia, not the U.S. South: the story centers on Benkos Bioho, who escaped slavery and built the maroon village San Basilio de Palenque in the 17th century, reportedly having women create 'maps' and deliver messages through cornrows (https://www.ancient-origins.net/weird-facts/braids-0017595, https://www.snopes.com/news/2022/03/12/maps-cornrows-black-slaves-escape/). A 2026 review at https://caro.news/how-cornrows-may-have-helped-free-slaves-navigate/ states plainly that 'the precise role of cornrows in aiding escapes during slavery is debated' and that 'no conclusive evidence has been found to directly confirm that enslaved people used cornrows as a systematic code for escape,' while noting historian Patricia Turner (UCLA folklorist) 'caution[s] against categorically declaring these practices true.'

Regarding the food/seed-storage claim, UCLA geography professor Judith Carney's book 'Black Rice' is frequently cited as the closest thing to scholarly backing, but even that source states (per Snopes) that 'the use of hair to convey messages or hide grains of rice is so prevalent in oral retellings that the lack of documentation feels beside the point' — i.e., an acknowledgment that it is oral tradition, not documented historical fact, and Carney's own research focused on rice origins in Suriname, not literal braid-smuggling in the US context.

Overall: this is a sympathetic, widely repeated legend that captures real themes of enslaved people's resilience and ingenuity, but lacks primary documentary evidence. Reputable fact-checkers (Snopes, Truth or Fiction) classify it as unverified folklore rather than established history, and some iterations of the story (especially Colombia-specific) are conflated into generalized claims about U.S. slavery and the Underground Railroad. The tweet presents the claim as settled fact ('Did you know...') without noting this crucial unverified/folkloric status, which a community note could clarify.

Seed/food claim has stronger academic support: Judith Carney in Black Rice (Harvard University Press, 2001) and With Grains in Her Hair argued African agency, noting "Legends passed down over generations recount how women hid rice grains, which could serve as seeds if they were still husked, in their hair before boarding the ships" https://www.sapiens.org/culture/african-rice-new-world/ ; SAPIENS notes Carney got criticism for "no smoking gun" because no enslaver records admit enslaved taught rice growing https://www.sapiens.org/culture/african-rice-new-world/ ; Maroon ethnobotany work records French agronomist Vaillant in 1948 mentioning "a legend that female ancestors had hidden rice in their hair in Africa and thus transported it to French Guiana" and anthropologist Marie Fleury documenting Aluku stories that "ancestors had found rice growing wild" but also "African women who before boarding slave ships hid grains of rice in their hair and thus transported rice from Africa to America" https://assets-eu.researchsquare.com/files/rs-4108655/v1/e539ad64-547f-436d-822b-ffe9921be1c2.pdf?c=1711116630 . Post overgeneralizes a Colombia-specific oral history as general runaway-slave practice and states contested map use as settled fact.
